title: EML trees: zero-equivalence and root existence are undecidable, assuming Richardson's theorem
abstract: The binary operator eml(x, y) = exp(x) - ln(y), with the constant 1 and a variable x, generates the elementary functions (Odrzywolek, arXiv:2603.21852). We formalize, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, a computable translation of Richardson expressions (built from rationals, pi, ln 2, x, +, *, sin, exp and |.|) into EML trees evaluated over the complex numbers with the principal logarithm. The translation preserves the value at every real x, including 0 and negative values, and no compiled tree ever applies log to 0 at any real input. Consequently, assuming Richardson's theorem as an explicit hypothesis, deciding whether an EML tree is identically zero on the reals, and deciding whether it has a real root, are both not computable. Both results also hold when log 0 is left undefined or is assigned any fixed value, so they do not depend on a convention for log 0. With the same compiler, three further problems are undecidable under the same hypothesis: whether two EML trees agree at every real x, whether a tree takes a negative real value at some real x, and whether a tree is constant on the reals (using continuity of Richardson expressions). The delicate part is controlling the branch cuts of the complex logarithm: signed arithmetic is carried out through positive quantities, pi and sin are obtained through complex values with imaginary parts kept inside (-pi, pi], and the absolute value is computed as a times the sign of a, where the sign is read off the branch cut of log without ever taking log 0.
